title: Association Cortex, Language, and the EEG
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the association cortex, the large regions outside the primary sensory and motor areas that combine information into planned behavior, attention, language, and recognition. It explains the prefrontal cortex and its circuits, the parietal attention system, the dominant-hemisphere language network, the dorsal and ventral visual streams, and how the scalp electroencephalogram (EEG) reflects arousal and sleep. Board questions usually describe a behavior, speech pattern, or perceptual deficit after a stroke, injury, or degenerative disease and ask you to localize it, or give EEG features and ask for the state. If you can name the network a symptom depends on and the artery that supplies it, you can localize most cortical syndromes.
prerequisites: Lobes, gyri, and sulci of the cerebral hemispheres and the main Brodmann areas (NE-3)
The visual pathway from retina to primary visual cortex and visual field defects (NE-6)
Territories of the anterior, middle, and posterior cerebral arteries (NE-10)

connections.how: Orbitofrontal and cingulate cortex work with limbic circuits for reward and emotion, and hypothalamic nuclei switch the brain between the waking and sleeping states the EEG records.
Aphasia, neglect, Gerstmann syndrome, and prosopagnosia are classic stroke syndromes localized by the divisions of the MCA and by the PCA.
Frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer disease are told apart by which association cortex degenerates first.
Both visual streams begin in primary visual cortex, so higher visual deficits must be separated from field defects caused by lesions earlier in the pathway.
Dopamine tunes prefrontal working memory, and acetylcholine, norepinephrine, serotonin, histamine, and orexin set arousal and the timing of REM sleep.

terms.def: Cortex outside the primary sensory and motor areas that integrates information across modalities to support cognition and behavior.
The abilities that hold a goal in mind, plan steps toward it, monitor progress, and suppress responses that do not fit the context.
The brief, active holding and manipulation of information needed for the task at hand.
Repeating a response or strategy after it is no longer appropriate or has been shown to fail.
Loss of will and spontaneous action, with slowed and reduced behavior even though the person can act when prompted.
Failure to attend or respond to stimuli on the side opposite a brain lesion that a primary sensory or motor deficit does not explain.
Unawareness or denial of one's own neurological deficit.
An acquired disorder of language affecting speaking, understanding, reading, or writing, distinct from a motor disorder of articulation.
A speech error in which a wrong sound (phonemic) or a wrong word (semantic) is substituted for the intended one.
Failure to recognize a stimulus despite intact primary sensation, attention, and language.
A brief burst of about 11 to 16 Hz waves generated by thalamocortical circuits and characteristic of N2 sleep.
A large, sharp, biphasic EEG wave of N2 sleep that can occur spontaneously or after a sound.

sections.title: Prefrontal cortex, executive function, and frontotemporal dementia

blocks.text: Normal structure and function

The prefrontal cortex is the part of the frontal lobe in front of the motor and premotor areas. It receives highly processed input from posterior association cortex, the limbic system, and the mediodorsal nucleus of the thalamus, and projects back to all of them. Its work is executive function: holding a goal in working memory, planning the steps toward it, shifting strategy when the situation changes, and suppressing actions that do not fit the context. Orbitofrontal cortex adds judgment and social conduct, which observers recognize as personality.

Each prefrontal region runs a parallel loop through the basal ganglia and thalamus that sustains the selected plan and inhibits competing ones. Dopamine from the ventral tegmental area (the mesocortical pathway) modulates dorsolateral working memory, so prefrontal performance is sensitive to dopamine level.

blocks.title: A frontal-subcortical loop
steps: Prefrontal cortex excites the caudate nucleus
Caudate inhibits the internal globus pallidus
Pallidal inhibition of the thalamus is released
Mediodorsal and ventral anterior thalamus re-excite the same cortex
Selected plan is sustained; competing plans are suppressed
blocks.caption: Simplified direct pathway. Damage anywhere in the loop, including the caudate or mediodorsal thalamus, can mimic a frontal lobe syndrome.

blocks.title: Prefrontal regions and the effects of damage
rows: Poor planning and organization, perseveration, concrete thinking
Lateral frontal tumor or MCA infarct, FTD
Linking actions to reward and social rules
Disinhibition, impulsivity, poor judgment, socially inappropriate behavior
Apathy and abulia; akinetic mutism if bilateral
blocks.caption: Most real lesions involve more than one region, so mixed pictures are common.

blocks.text: Pathophysiology and manifestations

Frontal damage rarely lowers scores on simple tests of knowledge; it disrupts the use of knowledge. A patient can state the rules yet break them, repeat a strategy after it stops working, or sit inactive while remaining able to act when prompted. Orbitofrontal contusions are common after head injury because the orbital surface strikes the irregular floor of the anterior cranial fossa. Large frontal lesions also release primitive reflexes (grasp, snout, palmomental) that frontal inhibition normally suppresses after infancy.
Frontotemporal dementia

Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a neurodegenerative disease that selectively destroys frontal and anterior temporal cortex, usually beginning between about 45 and 65 years. In the behavioral variant, disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive behaviors, and hyperorality (overeating, a craving for sweets) appear while memory and visuospatial skill are relatively preserved early. This is the reverse of Alzheimer disease, which begins in the medial temporal lobe and presents with memory loss. Other variants begin with progressive language decline (primary progressive aphasia). Imaging shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, sometimes so severe that the gyri are knife-thin.

The pathology is frontotemporal lobar degeneration with neuronal inclusions of tau or TDP-43, and rarely FUS. Pick disease is a tau subtype with round, silver-staining Pick bodies and swollen (ballooned) neurons. Familial cases often involve mutations in MAPT (tau) or GRN (progranulin), or a hexanucleotide repeat expansion in C9orf72, which also causes amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and explains why FTD and motor neuron disease can occur together.

sections.title: Parietal association cortex, spatial attention, neglect, and Gerstmann syndrome

blocks.text: Normal structure and function

The posterior parietal cortex lies behind the postcentral gyrus. The intraparietal sulcus divides it into the superior parietal lobule and the inferior parietal lobule, which contains the supramarginal and angular gyri. It combines visual, somatosensory, proprioceptive, and vestibular input into maps of space centered on the body, head, and eyes, and, with the frontal eye fields, selects which part of that space receives attention and guides the eyes and hand toward it.

Attention is lateralized. The left parietal lobe directs attention mainly to the right half of space, whereas the right parietal lobe attends to both halves. A right-lateralized network centered on the temporoparietal junction also detects unexpected events and reorients attention toward them. A left parietal lesion is therefore largely compensated by the intact right hemisphere, but a right parietal lesion leaves the left half of space with little attention, and the unopposed left hemisphere pulls attention further to the right.
Hemispatial neglect

Hemispatial neglect most often follows a right inferior parietal or temporoparietal infarct in the territory of the inferior division of the right MCA, although right frontal, thalamic, and basal ganglia lesions can also cause it. The patient eats from only the right side of the plate, shaves only the right face, marks the center of a line to the right of true center, and draws a clock with the numbers crowded onto the right. Extinction, missing the left stimulus only when both sides are stimulated together, is a milder form. Anosognosia often accompanies neglect, so the patient may deny left-sided weakness.

Neglect differs from homonymous hemianopia. A patient with a field cut knows that half the field is missing and turns the eyes and head to compensate, whereas a patient with neglect does not search the left side even when the visual fields are full. A large right MCA stroke can cause both.
Gerstmann syndrome

The dominant angular gyrus lies where the parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes meet, linking written symbols and numbers with language and the body schema. Damage, usually from an infarct in the inferior division of the left MCA or a tumor, causes Gerstmann syndrome: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia (inability to identify one's own fingers), and left-right confusion. The pure tetrad is rare; most patients also have alexia, anomia, or a fluent aphasia because Wernicke area is adjacent. Damage to the nearby dominant supramarginal gyrus can cause ideomotor apraxia, inability to perform a learned movement on command despite intact strength and comprehension.

blocks.title: Nondominant versus dominant parietal lesions
rows: Anosognosia, extinction, dressing and constructional apraxia
Alexia, anomia, fluent aphasia, ideomotor apraxia
Visual field if optic radiation is involved
blocks.caption: Primary sensory and field deficits are contralateral on either side; the attention and symbol deficits depend on which hemisphere is damaged.

blocks.predict: Why does a large left parietal stroke rarely cause lasting right-sided neglect, while a right parietal stroke of the same size often causes left-sided neglect?
blocks.explain: The right hemisphere attends to both halves of space, so after a left lesion it still covers the right side. The left hemisphere attends mainly to the right side, so after a right lesion nothing covers the left side well, and the unopposed left hemisphere biases attention rightward.

sections.title: The language network and the aphasias

blocks.text: Normal structure and function

Aphasia affects speaking, understanding, reading, and writing. It differs from dysarthria, a motor disorder of articulation in which language is intact and writing is normal. Language is lateralized to the left hemisphere in about 95% of right-handed people and most left-handed people, and that hemisphere is called dominant.

Broca area occupies the pars opercularis and pars triangularis of the dominant inferior frontal gyrus (Brodmann 44 and 45), just in front of the face and larynx region of the motor cortex, and assembles grammar and the motor plan for speech. Wernicke area lies in the posterior dominant superior temporal gyrus (posterior Brodmann 22), beside primary auditory cortex, and links sound patterns to word meaning. The arcuate fasciculus connects them, arching around the end of the lateral sulcus deep to the supramarginal gyrus.

blocks.title: Hearing and repeating a word
steps: Primary auditory cortex receives the sound
Wernicke area decodes it into a word
Arcuate fasciculus carries the word to Broca area
Broca area builds the speech motor plan
Motor cortex drives larynx, tongue, and lips
blocks.caption: Repetition needs the whole loop, so perisylvian lesions impair it.

blocks.text: Lesions and their manifestations

A Broca lesion, usually from the superior division of the left MCA, produces nonfluent aphasia: slow, effortful, telegraphic speech with few grammatical words, and impaired repetition and naming. Everyday comprehension is preserved, though grammatically complex sentences are often misunderstood. Because intact Wernicke area monitors the output, the patient recognizes the errors and is frustrated. Nearby motor cortex explains the frequent right face and arm weakness.

A Wernicke lesion, usually from the inferior division of the left MCA, produces fluent speech with normal rate and melody but little meaning, full of paraphasias and neologisms (invented words). Comprehension and repetition are impaired. Because the same area monitors the patient's own speech, the patient is often unaware of the problem and may seem confused. Weakness is usually absent, but involvement of the temporal optic radiation (Meyer loop) can cause a right superior quadrantanopia.

Conduction aphasia follows damage to the arcuate fasciculus or supramarginal gyrus. Speech is fluent with phonemic paraphasias and comprehension is good, but repetition is disproportionately poor because heard words cannot be passed forward; patients are aware of their errors. Global aphasia follows a large left MCA stem or internal carotid occlusion that destroys the whole network, usually with right hemiplegia and hemisensory loss. The transcortical aphasias, typically from watershed infarcts that spare the perisylvian loop, are the opposite case: repetition is preserved although fluency, comprehension, or both fail.

blocks.title: Classifying the aphasias
rows: Dominant inferior frontal gyrus (MCA superior division)
Dominant posterior superior temporal gyrus (MCA inferior division)
Whole perisylvian network (MCA stem or ICA)
Watershed cortex around the perisylvian loop
blocks.caption: Ask three questions: is speech fluent, is comprehension intact, and can the patient repeat?

blocks.title: Localizing an aphasia step by step
blocks.text: A 70-year-old speaks rapidly with normal melody but says "I took the plinder to the vorn," follows no spoken commands, and cannot repeat. Strength is normal, but the right upper quadrant of vision is lost. Fluent speech spares Broca area, and normal strength spares the motor strip. Impaired comprehension excludes conduction aphasia, and impaired repetition excludes transcortical sensory aphasia, leaving Wernicke aphasia. The quadrantanopia means the lesion reaches Meyer loop in the left temporal lobe: an infarct in the inferior division of the left MCA.

blocks.predict: After prolonged hypotension during surgery, a patient speaks little and with effort but repeats long sentences perfectly. Why is repetition spared?
blocks.explain: A watershed infarct between the ACA and MCA territories damaged frontal cortex near Broca area but spared the perisylvian loop itself. This is transcortical motor aphasia.

sections.title: Dorsal and ventral visual association streams

blocks.text: Normal structure and function

Primary visual cortex (V1, Brodmann 17), on the banks of the calcarine sulcus, maps the opposite visual field point by point but does not identify objects. Its output reaches association cortex along two broad routes. The dorsal stream runs upward into posterior parietal cortex and determines where an object is, how it moves, and how to act on it. The ventral stream runs downward into inferior occipitotemporal cortex and determines what the object is. The dorsal stream draws mainly on the magnocellular system (fast, motion-sensitive, little color), and the ventral stream mainly on the parvocellular system (fine detail and color), although the two interact.

blocks.title: The two visual association streams
rows: Where is it, and how do I act on it?
V4, fusiform gyrus, inferior temporal cortex
MCA, with the parieto-occipital MCA and PCA border zone
blocks.caption: Both streams start in V1; deficits in either occur with normal or near-normal acuity.

blocks.text: Dorsal stream lesions

Key dorsal areas include the motion area MT (V5) near the occipitotemporal junction on the lateral surface, and regions along the intraparietal sulcus that convert visual location into coordinates for reaching and eye movements. Bilateral MT damage causes akinetopsia, in which motion is seen as a series of still frames. Bilateral parieto-occipital damage, often from watershed infarcts between the MCA and PCA, causes Balint syndrome: simultanagnosia (seeing only one object at a time), optic ataxia (misreaching for objects that are clearly seen), and oculomotor apraxia (difficulty directing gaze voluntarily).
Ventral stream lesions and prosopagnosia

The ventral stream passes through V4, which is important for color, to inferior temporal cortex, where neurons respond to whole objects regardless of size or position. On the ventral surface, the fusiform gyrus contains the fusiform face area, which responds selectively to faces and is usually larger on the right. This region is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery. Damage, typically bilateral or right-sided, causes prosopagnosia, inability to recognize familiar faces. The patient sees and can describe the face but cannot say whose it is, yet recognizes the same person instantly by voice, gait, or clothing because knowledge of the person is intact. Nearby lesions cause achromatopsia (cortical loss of color vision) and visual object agnosia, and damage to the left fusiform region contributes to alexia.

blocks.title: Recognizing a familiar face
steps: Retina, lateral geniculate nucleus, and V1 encode edges and contrast
V2 and V4 assemble shape and color
Fusiform face area builds the configuration of the face
Anterior temporal cortex matches it to a stored identity
Name and personal knowledge are retrieved
blocks.caption: Prosopagnosia arises when the fusiform step fails; recognition by voice uses an auditory route and survives.

blocks.text: Because the streams are anatomically separate, lesions dissociate them. A patient with ventral damage may fail to recognize an object yet reach for it and shape the hand correctly, whereas a patient with optic ataxia names the object but misreaches. Normal acuity separates these higher deficits from lesions of the eye, optic nerve, or V1.

sections.title: EEG patterns, arousal, and sleep stages

blocks.text: What the EEG records

The scalp electroencephalogram records voltage produced by summed excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials in the apical dendrites of cortical pyramidal neurons, aligned perpendicular to the surface so their currents add. The pattern therefore reports synchrony: when many neurons receive the same rhythmic input, waves are slow and large; when each processes different information, waves are fast and small.
Regulation of arousal and sleep

Wakefulness is maintained by the ascending arousal system: cholinergic neurons of the pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental nuclei that activate the thalamus, and monoaminergic neurons (locus coeruleus norepinephrine, raphe serotonin, tuberomammillary histamine) that project widely to cortex, all stabilized by orexin (hypocretin) from the lateral hypothalamus. This input depolarizes thalamocortical neurons so they relay information faithfully, and the cortex desynchronizes into beta activity. At sleep onset, GABAergic neurons of the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus inhibit the arousal centers, and the thalamus shifts into rhythmic burst firing.

blocks.title: From wakefulness to slow-wave sleep
steps: Ventrolateral preoptic GABA neurons inhibit arousal centers
Cholinergic and monoamine drive to the thalamus falls
Thalamocortical neurons hyperpolarize; T-type Ca2+ channels recover
Thalamic reticular nucleus paces bursts: spindles in N2
Deeper hyperpolarization slows the rhythm: delta waves in N3
blocks.caption: Sleep synchronizes the cortex by changing thalamic firing mode.

blocks.text: Sleep stages

Relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed produces posterior alpha, which disappears when the eyes open. N1 replaces alpha with theta and slow rolling eye movements. N2, the largest share of the night, adds spindles and K complexes. N3, or slow-wave sleep, has high-amplitude delta, the highest arousal threshold, and the nightly peak of growth hormone; sleepwalking and sleep terrors arise from it. REM sleep shows a low-voltage, mixed-frequency EEG resembling wakefulness, with rapid eye movements, dreaming, and atonia of skeletal muscle except the extraocular muscles and diaphragm.

blocks.title: EEG by state
blocks.caption: Amplitude rises and frequency falls as non-REM sleep deepens; REM returns to a waking-like pattern.

blocks.text: REM is generated by pontine cholinergic REM-on neurons when locus coeruleus and raphe REM-off neurons fall silent. Atonia comes from pontine neurons that drive medullary glycinergic and GABAergic inhibition of motor neurons; failure of this pathway causes dream enactment (REM sleep behavior disorder). Non-REM and REM alternate in cycles of about 90 minutes, with N3 concentrated in the first third and REM periods lengthening toward morning. REM latency, normally about 90 minutes, is shortened in narcolepsy (loss of orexin neurons) and in depression.

blocks.title: Identifying a REM epoch
blocks.text: A 30-second epoch shows low-voltage, mixed-frequency activity, bursts of rapid eye movements, and an almost flat chin electromyogram. Low-voltage, mixed-frequency activity fits wakefulness, N1, or REM. The flat chin electromyogram means atonia, which wakefulness and N1 lack, and the eye movements are rapid rather than the slow rolling movements of N1, so the epoch is REM. If it appeared within 15 minutes of sleep onset, the short REM latency would suggest narcolepsy, in which loss of orexin lets REM intrude early.

blocks.predict: Why do sleepwalking and sleep terrors cluster in the first third of the night, while dream enactment in REM sleep behavior disorder clusters in the last third?
blocks.explain: Sleepwalking and terrors are partial arousals from N3, which dominates the early cycles. REM periods lengthen toward morning, so a disorder of REM atonia appears mostly late.

integration.text: Anatomy and pathology meet through blood supply and degeneration. The superior division of the left MCA supplies Broca area and the lateral frontal lobe, the inferior division supplies Wernicke area, the angular gyrus, and, on the right, the parietal cortex whose loss causes neglect. The ACA supplies medial frontal cortex (abulia), the PCA supplies the fusiform gyrus (prosopagnosia, alexia), and border zones produce transcortical aphasias and Balint syndrome. Degenerative disease follows networks rather than arteries: FTD begins in frontal and anterior temporal cortex with tau or TDP-43 inclusions, typical Alzheimer disease begins in the medial temporal lobe, and its posterior cortical variant can present with dorsal stream deficits.

Physiology and biochemistry explain the EEG and arousal. The EEG reflects synaptic currents and thalamic firing mode, which are set by acetylcholine, monoamines, histamine, orexin, and GABA, so drugs and metabolic disorders that change these transmitters change the EEG and the state of arousal. The localizations in this chapter are models: lateralization is statistical, the visual streams interact, and real lesions often combine features, so a clinical picture is localized by its dominant pattern rather than by a single sign.

summary: Prefrontal cortex supports working memory, planning, judgment, and impulse control through loops with the basal ganglia and thalamus.
Dorsolateral damage causes poor planning and perseveration, orbitofrontal damage causes disinhibition, and medial frontal damage causes apathy and abulia.
Frontotemporal dementia begins with behavior or language change while memory is relatively spared, with tau (including Pick bodies) or TDP-43 inclusions.
The right parietal lobe attends to both sides of space, so a right parietal lesion causes left hemispatial neglect, often with anosognosia.
A dominant angular gyrus lesion causes Gerstmann syndrome: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and left-right confusion.
Broca aphasia is nonfluent with intact comprehension, Wernicke aphasia is fluent with impaired comprehension, conduction aphasia selectively impairs repetition, and global aphasia impairs all three.
Repetition fails with perisylvian lesions and is spared in transcortical aphasias from watershed infarcts.
The dorsal stream (occipitoparietal) handles location, motion, and reaching; the ventral stream (occipitotemporal) handles object and face recognition, and fusiform damage causes prosopagnosia.
The EEG reflects cortical synchrony: beta awake, alpha relaxed with eyes closed, theta in N1, spindles and K complexes in N2, delta in N3, and low-voltage beta-like activity in REM.
REM combines a waking-like EEG with rapid eye movements and atonia; N3 dominates early night and REM lengthens toward morning.

verify: Language dominance figures (about 95% of right-handed people left-dominant; most left-handed people, often quoted as about 60% to 70%) vary between sources.
Typical age of onset of FTD (about 45 to 65 years) and the relative frequency of tau versus TDP-43 pathology vary among series.
Sleep stage percentages, spindle frequency (about 11 to 16 Hz, often taught as 12 to 14 Hz), and the beta range (above 13 Hz, sometimes 14 to 30 Hz) differ slightly between texts and with age.
Whether prosopagnosia requires bilateral fusiform damage or can follow a right-sided lesion alone is stated differently by sources; this chapter says bilateral or right-sided.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Broca, Wernicke, Gerstmann, Balint, Pick, and Meyer loop, and the transcortical aphasias, or only the four aphasias named in the competency.
